Max Common Chord 6

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: two circles meet at P and Q, and a straight line through P cuts a piece AB between them that can be made bigger or smaller.
How to play: Drag A or B to slide the line, or drag P or Q to change the circles; focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Pick “circles” or “chord”, tick “names”, or press “Show the best chord”.
Drag:
Look for the math

Two answers to a 1975 olympiad problem look unrelated: one uses angles, the other uses a circle through the two circle centres. This drawing shows why they are the same answer.

Turn the product into one distance

Let the line through P meet the first circle again at A and the second at B. The intersecting chords theorem says AP × PB = PQ × PR, where R is the second meeting of the circumcircle of A, B, Q with the line PQ. PQ is fixed, so making the product biggest is the same as pushing R as far as possible along PQ. Since R is the mirror of Q in the foot N of the perpendicular from the circle's centre S to PQ, that distance is twice QN. It is largest when SN just touches the circle C(O) through the two original centres and Q — that is, when the radius OS is parallel to PQ.

The final touch

At that chosen S, the point W where AE meets BF lies on both C(O) and the circle C(S) centred at S through Q. The line RW is a diameter of C(S), so the angles RAW and RBW are right angles, by Thales' theorem. Because A, R, E are lined up with the first tangent direction (and B, R, F with the second), RA and RB are tangents to the two given circles. That condition is exactly the angle answer: ∠EPA = ∠FPB.

The other route

Hubert Shutrick also noticed that SW is perpendicular to AB. Since S is equally far from A and B, W is the midpoint of AB. The line through E parallel to AB then cuts the angle at Q in half, and the same equal angles at P come out again. Press “names” to see W, S and R, and press “Show the best chord” to put the chord where both routes agree.

What was checked

The original page is a fill-in-the-blank discussion; its blank about the two angles subtended by a diameter is answered “right”. The logic test compares the drawing with a second transcription of the applet's own construction in 600 layouts, and in 120 of them checks the collinearity, equal radii, tangency, W, diameter and equal-angle claims. A scan of 1,440 directions in 30 layouts finds no chord with a larger product than the one C(S) gives. The applet has only two checkboxes; the best-chord button here is a reading aid and changes none of the rules.

Try this: press “Show the best chord”, tick “names”, then choose “circles” and drag A. Watch how the matching chord moves as the two circles change.
